generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this shows up in the line between the results and the discussion. Across any subject, the results report what was found, the figures and the tests, plainly and without interpretation. The discussion is where you say what the findings mean, how far they can be trusted, and how they sit against existing work. Reporting a measured difference in the results is right; writing 'this proves the idea works' into the results is the error this lesson targets.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students writing up the same small study, who reach the results section.

Student A writes that the scores were higher in the second group, which shows the treatment clearly works and that the usual approach is a mistake. The finding is there, but it is tangled with interpretation and a recommendation. A reader cannot see the plain result on its own, and claims about what it means have arrived before the discussion, where they could be weighed.

Student B writes, in the results, that the second group scored higher on average, by a stated margin and with the relevant test. Student B saves the reading of that difference for the discussion. There they ask whether the margin is large enough to matter, note that the sample was small and drawn from one setting, and hold back from advising anyone until the evidence can bear it.

Both found the same result. Only Student B kept the results and the discussion in their proper sections.
generatedProse.summary: A report is structured so that each core element does one job: the introduction frames the question, the methodology makes the work repeatable, the results present the findings, and the discussion interprets them. You can now use these elements for their proper purpose, tell results apart from discussion, and place a passage in the section where it belongs. With the review, the proposal and the report, you have the three genres that carry research in any field.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Student B do that Student A did not?

items.text: Student B reported the finding plainly in the results and saved its interpretation for the discussion.
Student B found a larger difference between the two groups.
Student B recommended changing practice more strongly than Student A.
Student B wrote a longer results section than Student A.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B kept the plain finding in the results and its interpretation in the discussion.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look at WHERE each student put the finding and its interpretation.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B reported the finding in the results and saved interpretation for the discussion. A bigger difference, a stronger recommendation or more length were not the point.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
